title: Getting by: greeting people and being polite
intro: Fixed formulas rather than words you build from parts. Learn each one whole. Spanish is warmer than English here: strangers greet each other in lifts and shops, and skipping the greeting reads as rudeness rather than efficiency.

entries.note: Neutral at any hour and with anyone. The h is silent.
Plural in Spanish, always. Used until about midday.

ex.en: Good morning, have you had breakfast?

entries.note: From midday until dark, so it covers the English evening too.

ex.es: Buenas tardes, ¿en qué le puedo ayudar?
ex.en: Good afternoon, how can I help you?

entries.note: One phrase for both hello and goodbye after dark — the moment decides which.

ex.en: Good evening, a table for two.

entries.en: how are you? (informal); how are you? (formal)
entries.note: The -s ending is the whole difference between tú and usted.

ex.en: Good morning, doctor. How are you?

entries.note: Casual and invariable — no verb to conjugate, which makes it the safe one.
bien is an adverb, bueno an adjective. Estoy bien, not estoy bueno — the second means something quite different.

ex.es: Cuesta más o menos cien pesos.
ex.en: It costs about a hundred pesos.

entries.note: muchas gracias, never mucho gracias — the word is feminine plural.

ex.en: Thank you very much for everything.

entries.note: In Mexico you will also hear no hay de qué and con gusto.

entries.en: sorry; excuse me (to get past or interrupt)

ex.en: Sorry, I didn't mean to bother you.
Excuse me, may I get past?

entries.note: The opener for asking a stranger anything. Informal: disculpa.

ex.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

entries.note: Said as you squeeze past someone or step away from a table. Where English says nothing, Spanish says this.

ex.es: Con permiso, voy a salir un momento.
ex.en: Excuse me, I'm going to step out for a moment.

entries.note: The reply is igualmente or el gusto es mío.

ex.en: Nice to meet you, I'm Miguel.

entries.note: claro que sí is an emphatic yes; claro que no an emphatic no.
Literally health. The same word covers the toast and the sneeze.
A touch final. For everyday partings people prefer hasta luego or chao.

ex.en: Goodbye, and have a good trip.

entries.note: Same pattern: hasta mañana, hasta el lunes, hasta pronto.
